description: A BGCTUB 2nd-semester BEE (Basic Electrical Engineering) course. In-scope chapters (per syllabus): ch1–ch4, ch6 (capacitors), ch7 (RC transients). Other chapters present in this file are out-of-scope reference material kept for completeness.

chapters.title: Basic Concepts

topics.title: Introduction to Electric Circuits
topics.body:
An **electric circuit** is an interconnection of electrical elements through which current can flow. Every circuit contains at least one source (battery, generator, signal generator) and at least one element that uses or stores energy (resistor, capacitor, inductor, lamp, motor).

Circuit analysis lets us predict how a given network will behave — what currents will flow, what voltages will appear, how much power will be dissipated — before we build it. The mathematical tools we use throughout this course rest on three foundations:

- **Ohm's law** — relates voltage, current, and resistance in a passive element.
- **Kirchhoff's laws (KCL, KVL)** — express the conservation of charge and energy at every node and around every loop.
- **The element i-v relationships** — describe what each component does (linear for R, L, C; nonlinear for diodes, transistors, etc.).
pitfalls: Confusing electrical engineering's 'circuit' (a graph of elements) with a physical PCB layout.
Treating wires in idealised schematics as having resistance — assume zero unless stated.

topics.title: Systems of Units (SI)
topics.body:
Engineering uses the **International System of Units (SI)**. The six base units that show up everywhere in electrical engineering are:

| Quantity | Unit | Symbol |
|---|---|---|
| Length | metre | m |
| Mass | kilogram | kg |
| Time | second | s |
| Current | ampere | A |
| Temperature | kelvin | K |
| Luminous intensity | candela | cd |

Every other electrical quantity is **derived** from these. Voltage, charge, energy, and power are all combinations of the base units.

Decimal multiples appear constantly. Memorise these prefixes — questions and component values will assume you read them fluently:

| Prefix | Symbol | Multiplier |
|---|---|---|
| giga | G | $10^{9}$ |
| mega | M | $10^{6}$ |
| kilo | k | $10^{3}$ |
| milli | m | $10^{-3}$ |
| micro | µ | $10^{-6}$ |
| nano | n | $10^{-9}$ |
| pico | p | $10^{-12}$ |

examples.q: Convert 4700 µF to farads.

pitfalls: Mixing up M (mega, $10^6$) with m (milli, $10^{-3}$) — they differ by a factor of $10^9$.
Writing 'mA' when you meant 'µA' on small-current questions. Always sanity-check magnitudes.

topics.title: Charge and Current
topics.body:
**Charge** is the basic electrical quantity. The SI unit is the coulomb (C). One electron carries $e = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}$ C, so it takes about $6.24 \times 10^{18}$ electrons to make 1 C.

**Current** is the rate of flow of charge past a point:

$$i = \dfrac{dq}{dt}$$

The SI unit is the ampere (A) where $1 \text{ A} = 1 \text{ C/s}$. When current is constant in time (DC) the integral form is simpler:

$$Q = i \cdot t$$

**Conventional current** points in the direction positive charge would move — opposite to the actual flow of electrons in a metal wire. Every formula in this course uses conventional current. Just remember: the labelled arrow on a schematic shows where positive charge moves, electrons go the other way.

examples.q: A current of 2 A flows through a wire for 5 minutes. How much charge passes through?
How many electrons constitute 1 C of charge?

pitfalls: Forgetting that conventional current is *opposite* to electron flow in metals.
Mixing up coulombs (Q) with amperes (i). 'Coulombs per second' is the ampere — not the other way around.

topics.title: Voltage
topics.body:
**Voltage** (also called **potential difference** or **electromotive force, EMF**) is the energy required to move a unit of positive charge from one point to another:

$$v = \dfrac{dw}{dq}$$

Unit: volt (V), where $1 \text{ V} = 1 \text{ J/C}$. A 12-V battery does 12 J of work for every coulomb of charge it pushes through the circuit.

Voltage is *always* a difference between two points. When we say 'the voltage at node A is 5 V' we implicitly mean *with respect to the reference node (ground)*. A single point cannot have an absolute voltage; voltage is between two points.

**Polarity** is shown on a schematic by + and − marks at the element's terminals. The voltage $v_{AB}$ means the voltage at A minus the voltage at B. Reversing the subscripts flips the sign: $v_{BA} = -v_{AB}$.

**EMF** (electromotive force) is the same thing as voltage measured at the terminals of a source. The name is historical — there is no actual force involved.

examples.q: If 30 J of energy is used to move 6 C of charge through a component, what is the voltage across it?

pitfalls: Stating 'the voltage at point X' without specifying the reference. Always say 'with respect to ground' or 'between X and Y'.
Forgetting polarity. $v_{AB} = -v_{BA}$ — sign matters when applying KVL.

topics.title: Power and Energy
topics.body:
**Power** is the rate of energy transfer:

$$p = \dfrac{dw}{dt} = v \cdot i$$

Unit: watt (W) = 1 J/s. Power can also be written in three equivalent forms when Ohm's law applies:

$$P = vi = i^{2}R = \dfrac{v^{2}}{R}$$

**Energy** is the integral of power over time:

$$w = \int_{t_0}^{t_1} p \, dt$$

For constant power, $w = P \cdot t$. Electricity bills measure energy in kilowatt-hours (kWh): 1 kWh = $3.6 \times 10^{6}$ J.

**Passive sign convention** — when current enters the *positive* terminal of an element, $P = v \cdot i$ is the power **absorbed** by that element. If the same product comes out negative, the element is actually **delivering** power. Sources (batteries) typically deliver power; resistors always absorb it.

examples.q: A 60-W light bulb is operated for 4 hours. At 8 BDT per kWh, what is the energy cost?
steps: Energy: $W = P \cdot t = 60 \text{ W} \times 4 \text{ h} = 240$ Wh = 0.24 kWh

examples.q: Find the power dissipated by a 220-Ω resistor carrying 0.5 A.

pitfalls: Confusing power (W) with energy (J or Wh). 'A 100 W bulb consumes 100 W per hour' is wrong — it consumes 100 W (continuously) and 100 Wh per hour.
Sign confusion in passive sign convention. Stick to the convention: arrow into +, then $P > 0$ means absorbing.

topics.title: Circuit Elements (Active vs Passive)
topics.body:
Every element in a circuit is either **active** or **passive**.

**Active elements** generate electrical energy. The four basic types are:

- **Independent voltage source** — maintains a specified voltage regardless of current. Schematic: a circle with + and −, or a battery symbol.
- **Independent current source** — maintains a specified current regardless of voltage. Schematic: a circle with an arrow.
- **Dependent (controlled) sources** — voltage or current is set by a *controlling variable* elsewhere in the circuit. Four flavours: VCVS, VCCS, CCVS, CCCS. Schematic: diamond-shaped.

**Passive elements** absorb or store energy but cannot generate it on their own. The three fundamental passive elements you'll meet this term are:

- **Resistor (R)** — dissipates electrical energy as heat. $v = iR$.
- **Capacitor (C)** — stores energy in an electric field. $i = C\,dv/dt$.
- **Inductor (L)** — stores energy in a magnetic field. $v = L\,di/dt$.

Real components are never perfectly ideal. A real resistor has tiny parasitic inductance and capacitance; a real battery has internal resistance that limits short-circuit current. For introductory circuit analysis we use the ideal models.
pitfalls: Treating a real battery as an ideal voltage source in all cases. For short-circuit and high-current questions, model it as $V_s$ in series with $R_\text{int}$.
Mistaking a dependent source's controlling variable. Always identify what variable it depends on before writing equations.

topics.title: Applications: Power Bills, Devices
topics.body:
**Electricity bills** are computed from energy consumption in kilowatt-hours. The bill = $\sum (\text{appliance power in kW}) \times (\text{hours used}) \times (\text{rate per kWh})$.

**Typical appliance power ratings** (approximate):

| Appliance | Power |
|---|---|
| LED bulb | 7–12 W |
| Ceiling fan | 60–80 W |
| TV (LED, 40") | 60–100 W |
| Laptop | 30–65 W |
| Refrigerator (running) | 100–200 W |
| Microwave | 800–1200 W |
| Electric kettle | 1500–2200 W |
| Air conditioner (1 ton) | 1000–1500 W |

**Why this matters in BEE**: every real-world circuit ultimately comes down to managing voltage, current, and power. Knowing typical magnitudes lets you sanity-check your calculations — if you compute 50 W for an LED bulb, you almost certainly have an error.

examples.q: A household runs four 80-W fans for 8 hours and ten 10-W bulbs for 5 hours daily. Monthly cost at 8 BDT/kWh (30 days)?
steps: Total per day = 3.06 kWh, per month = $3.06 \times 30 = 91.8$ kWh

topics.title: Problem Solving Methodology
topics.body:
Sadiku's six-step approach scales from this course all the way through circuit design:

1. **Carefully define the problem.** Read the question twice. Identify what's given and what's asked. Sketch the circuit if it isn't given.
2. **Present everything you know.** Mark known values on the schematic. Choose a reference node. Label every node and branch.
3. **Establish a set of alternative solutions.** Could you solve this by mesh, nodal, Thévenin, superposition, source transformation? Pick the one with fewest unknowns.
4. **Attempt a solution.** Write the equations. Solve them — by hand or matrix. Carry units through every step.
5. **Evaluate the solution.** Does the magnitude make sense? Did current go in the direction you expected? Check power balance: power supplied should equal power absorbed.
6. **Has the problem been solved satisfactorily?** If not, return to step 3 with a different method.

**The single most useful habit**: always check your answer with a *different* technique. If mesh analysis gives $i_1 = 3$ A, plug back into the original circuit and verify with KCL at a node you didn't use.
pitfalls: Skipping the sanity check. A wrong-by-a-factor-of-1000 answer is almost always a units mistake.
Solving without labelling nodes. You will lose track of polarity halfway through.

chapters.title: Basic Laws

topics.title: Ohm's Law
topics.body:
**Ohm's law** states that the voltage across a resistive element is directly proportional to the current through it:

$$v = i \cdot R$$

where $R$ is the **resistance** in ohms (Ω). One ohm is 1 V/A.

Resistance of a uniform conductor depends on geometry and material:

$$R = \dfrac{\rho \, L}{A}$$

$\rho$ is the **resistivity** of the material (Ω·m), $L$ is length, $A$ is cross-sectional area. Copper: $\rho \approx 1.72 \times 10^{-8}$ Ω·m; aluminium: $2.82 \times 10^{-8}$; nichrome (heating element): $1.10 \times 10^{-6}$.

**Conductance** $G = 1/R$ has units of siemens (S). High conductance = low resistance.

**Limitations.** Ohm's law applies only to **ohmic** (linear) materials within their rated range. It fails for:

- Diodes (exponential $i$-$v$ curve)
- Transistors (depend on gate voltage)
- Resistors at very high temperature (resistance rises with $T$)
- Discharge tubes, neon lamps (nonlinear conduction)

examples.q: A 220-Ω resistor has 11 V across it. Find the current.

pitfalls: Applying Ohm's law to a non-linear element (diode, transistor) — won't give correct results.
Forgetting to convert units. R in kΩ and i in mA gives v in volts — but only if you're consistent.

topics.title: Nodes, Branches, and Loops
topics.body:
These are the three structural pieces of any circuit. Every analysis method (KVL, KCL, mesh, nodal) starts by identifying them.

- **Branch** — a single two-terminal element (one resistor, one capacitor, one source, one wire segment).
- **Node** — a junction where *two or more* branches meet. Wires connecting nodes without an intervening element are part of the same node.
- **Loop** — any closed path through the circuit. An **independent loop** is one that contains at least one branch not in any other loop. **Mesh** is the term for a loop with no loops inside it (think 'window pane').

**Counting rule** — for a connected circuit with $b$ branches, $n$ nodes, and $\ell$ independent loops:

$$\ell = b - n + 1$$

This tells you exactly how many independent KVL equations you need to write. KCL gives you $n - 1$ independent equations (one node is redundant since charge in = charge out globally).

examples.q: A circuit has 8 branches and 5 nodes. How many independent loops does it have?

pitfalls: Counting nodes as 'every wire bend' — only true junctions count, plus the points where elements terminate.
Confusing mesh (smallest loop) with loop (any closed path). Mesh analysis uses meshes; KVL uses any loop.

topics.title: Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL)
topics.body:
**Kirchhoff's Current Law** is the statement of conservation of charge at every node:

$$\sum_{n=1}^{N} i_n = 0$$

The algebraic sum of all currents entering a node is zero. Equivalently: the sum of currents *in* equals the sum of currents *out*.

**Sign convention**: pick one direction (in or out) and call it positive. Currents flowing that direction are +; currents flowing the other way are −. Be consistent within each node equation.

**Why it works**: a node has no capacity to store charge. Whatever flows in must flow out, instant by instant. (Real wires can have tiny capacitance, but in ideal circuit analysis we ignore it.)

**KCL applies at every node** — but only $n-1$ of the $n$ node equations are independent. Skipping one (usually the ground/reference) gives you a non-redundant system.

examples.q: At a node, $i_1 = 3$ A and $i_2 = 4$ A flow in; $i_3 = 2$ A flows out. Find the fourth branch current $i_4$ (define + as out of node).

pitfalls: Mixing 'in' and 'out' signs within the same equation. Pick one convention per node and stick to it.
Forgetting that a current source forces a specific current — you don't compute it, you just use its value.

topics.title: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL)
topics.body:
**Kirchhoff's Voltage Law** is the statement of conservation of energy around every closed loop:

$$\sum_{n=1}^{N} v_n = 0$$

The algebraic sum of all voltages around any closed path is zero — energy gained equals energy spent.

**Sign convention**: walk around the loop in a chosen direction (clockwise or counter-clockwise). When you enter an element at its + terminal, write *+v*; when you enter at the − terminal, write *−v*. Sources work the same way: + to − across a source means an EMF rise.

**Why it works**: a charge taken once around any closed path returns to its starting potential. The net energy gained = net energy spent.

KVL with $\ell$ independent loops gives $\ell$ equations. Combined with $n-1$ KCL equations and $b$ Ohm's law element equations, you have enough to solve for every branch current and node voltage in any resistive network.

examples.q: A loop has a 24-V source, then voltage drops of 9 V across $R_1$, then $V_2$ across $R_2$, then 4 V across $R_3$, back to the source. Find $V_2$.
steps: KVL: source rise = sum of drops

pitfalls: Reversing the sign of a source when traversing it from − to +. Track polarity carefully — most KVL errors come from this.
Writing KVL for a path that isn't closed. A loop must end where it started.

topics.title: Series Resistors and Voltage Division
topics.body:
Two or more resistors are in **series** when they share a single connection and the same current flows through all of them. The equivalent resistance is the sum:

$$R_{eq} = R_1 + R_2 + \cdots + R_n$$

**Voltage Divider Rule (VDR).** When $n$ resistors in series share a source voltage $v$, each resistor takes a fraction of $v$ proportional to its own value:

$$v_k = \dfrac{R_k}{R_1 + R_2 + \cdots + R_n} \cdot v$$

For two resistors specifically:

$$v_1 = \dfrac{R_1}{R_1 + R_2} \cdot v, \quad v_2 = \dfrac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} \cdot v$$

**Use VDR when**: you need a voltage across one resistor in a series chain and don't want to compute the current first.

examples.q: A 12-V source feeds $R_1 = 4$ kΩ and $R_2 = 8$ kΩ in series. Find the voltage across $R_2$.

pitfalls: Applying VDR when current is being drawn through a third path. VDR assumes only the series chain — if a load is connected across one of the resistors, you need a Thévenin analysis instead.
Forgetting that the largest resistor in a series chain drops the most voltage.

topics.title: Parallel Resistors and Current Division
topics.body:
Two or more resistors are in **parallel** when their terminals share both nodes and the same voltage appears across all of them. Equivalent resistance:

$$\dfrac{1}{R_{eq}} = \dfrac{1}{R_1} + \dfrac{1}{R_2} + \cdots + \dfrac{1}{R_n}$$

For exactly two resistors, the *product-over-sum* form is faster:

$$R_{eq} = \dfrac{R_1 \, R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$$

Notice $R_{eq}$ is always *smaller* than the smallest of the parallel resistors.

**Current Divider Rule (CDR).** For two resistors in parallel sharing a total current $i$, the current through one of them is given by the *other's* resistance divided by the sum:

$$i_1 = \dfrac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} \cdot i, \quad i_2 = \dfrac{R_1}{R_1 + R_2} \cdot i$$

Current divides **inversely** with resistance — the smaller resistor takes more current.

examples.q: $R_1 = 6$ Ω and $R_2 = 12$ Ω are in parallel. Find $R_{eq}$, and the current through $R_1$ if the total current is 9 A.

pitfalls: Confusing the CDR sign — for the current through $R_1$, the numerator is $R_2$ (the OTHER resistor), not $R_1$.
Applying the product/sum form to three or more resistors. That shortcut only works for exactly two.

topics.title: Wye-Delta (Y-Δ) Transformations
topics.body:
Some networks aren't pure series/parallel — three resistors arranged in a triangle (Δ) or in a star (Y, also written T) can't be simplified directly. The **wye-delta transformation** converts between the two forms so the rest of the circuit can be reduced.

Label the three Δ resistors $R_a, R_b, R_c$ between three nodes 1, 2, 3 and the three Y resistors $R_1, R_2, R_3$ from the same three nodes meeting at a common centre node.

**Δ → Y** (use when the network has a triangle you want to simplify):

$$R_1 = \dfrac{R_b R_c}{R_a + R_b + R_c}, \quad R_2 = \dfrac{R_a R_c}{R_a + R_b + R_c}, \quad R_3 = \dfrac{R_a R_b}{R_a + R_b + R_c}$$

**Y → Δ** (use when the network has a Y/T you want to make into a Δ):

$$R_a = \dfrac{R_1 R_2 + R_2 R_3 + R_3 R_1}{R_1}$$

and similarly for $R_b$ (denominator $R_2$) and $R_c$ (denominator $R_3$).

**Symmetric special case**: when all three resistors are equal,

$$R_Y = \dfrac{R_\Delta}{3}, \quad R_\Delta = 3R_Y$$

examples.q: Convert a balanced Δ with each arm = 30 Ω to its Y equivalent.

pitfalls: Mixing up which Y resistor corresponds to which Δ pair. Each Y arm is opposite the Δ arm with the matching subscript — $R_1$ is opposite $R_a$.
Forgetting that the centre node of the Y didn't exist in the Δ — it's a virtual node introduced by the transformation.

topics.title: Applications: Lighting, DC Meters
topics.body:
**Lighting circuits.** Series Christmas-tree lights: if one bulb fails open, the whole string goes dark (no current path). Parallel household lighting: each bulb has its own path; one failing leaves the others lit. Trade-off: series uses less wire but is fragile; parallel costs more wire but is reliable.

**DC ammeter** measures current. It must be inserted **in series** with the branch you want to measure (so all the current flows through it). The ammeter's internal resistance must be very low so it doesn't disturb the circuit. A typical multimeter ammeter has $R_\text{shunt} \approx 0.1$ Ω.

**DC voltmeter** measures voltage. It must be connected **in parallel** with the element you want to measure (so it sees the same voltage). Its internal resistance must be very high so almost no current flows through it. A digital multimeter voltmeter has $R_\text{in} \approx 10$ MΩ.

**The cardinal sin**: connecting an ammeter directly across a voltage source. The ammeter's near-zero resistance becomes a short circuit and either blows a fuse or destroys the meter.
pitfalls: Inserting a voltmeter in series (you'll read tiny current and break the circuit) or an ammeter in parallel (instant short).
Ignoring the meter's internal resistance in precision measurements. A 1-MΩ resistor measured by a 10-MΩ voltmeter is 10% off.

topics.title: Nodal Analysis (Node Voltage Method)
topics.body:
**Nodal analysis** solves a circuit by finding the **voltage at every non-reference node** (with respect to ground). Once you know node voltages, every branch current follows from Ohm's law.

**Procedure**:

1. Choose a reference node (ground) — typically the one with the most branches. Label its voltage 0.
2. Assign a voltage variable $V_1, V_2, \ldots$ to each remaining node.
3. Apply **KCL at each non-reference node**. For a branch from node $i$ to node $j$ through resistance $R$, the current leaving node $i$ is $(V_i - V_j)/R$.
4. Solve the resulting linear system for $V_1, V_2, \ldots$.

**By inspection** — for a circuit with only resistors and independent current sources, the nodal equations can be written directly as $\mathbf{G}\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{I}_s$, where:

- $G_{kk}$ = sum of conductances connected to node $k$
- $G_{kj}$ = negative of conductance between nodes $k$ and $j$
- $I_{s,k}$ = total current source flowing **into** node $k$

Nodal is generally easier when **there are few nodes** relative to branches, or when most sources are **current sources**.

examples.q: A single node $V_A$ is fed by 10 V through 2 Ω and 6 V through 2 Ω; it drains through 4 Ω to ground. Find $V_A$.
steps: KCL at A (sum of currents into A = 0):

pitfalls: Forgetting to label the reference. Without ground at 0 V, your node voltages have no meaning.
Mixing 'into the node' and 'out of the node' signs. Pick one convention per node.

topics.title: Nodal Analysis with Voltage Sources (Supernodes)
topics.body:
When an **ideal voltage source** sits directly between two non-reference nodes, you can't write a standard KCL at either end — the source forces a relationship, not a passive current.

**The supernode technique**: treat the two nodes plus the voltage source between them as one big 'supernode'. KCL still applies to the boundary — currents into the supernode sum to zero — but you need a **constraint equation** for the voltage source:

$$V_i - V_j = V_s$$

where $V_s$ is the source voltage (sign per the source's polarity).

**Procedure**:

1. Identify supernodes (any pair of non-reference nodes joined by an ideal voltage source).
2. Write KCL for each supernode treating the two nodes as one.
3. Add the constraint equation $V_i - V_j = V_s$ for each supernode.
4. Write KCL normally at all other nodes.

If the voltage source is between a non-reference node and **ground**, it's even simpler — that node's voltage is *known* directly ($V_k = V_s$), so it doesn't need a KCL equation.
pitfalls: Forgetting to write the constraint $V_i - V_j = V_s$. Without it the system is under-determined.
Getting the constraint sign backward — check which node is at the + terminal of the source.

topics.title: Mesh Analysis (Mesh Current Method)
topics.body:
**Mesh analysis** solves a circuit by assigning a current variable to each mesh (the smallest closed loops, like window panes in a planar circuit) and applying KVL around each.

**Procedure**:

1. Identify the meshes. A planar circuit with $b$ branches and $n$ nodes has $\ell = b - n + 1$ meshes.
2. Assign a mesh current $i_1, i_2, \ldots, i_\ell$ to each, all in the same direction (clockwise by convention).
3. Write **KVL around each mesh**. For a resistor shared between two meshes, the actual current is the *difference* of the two mesh currents — be careful with signs.
4. Solve the linear system for $i_1, i_2, \ldots, i_\ell$.

**Branch current** through a shared element: if mesh 1 and mesh 2 both flow clockwise and share resistor $R$, then the branch current through $R$ from mesh 1's side is $i_1 - i_2$.

**By inspection** — for circuits with only resistors and independent voltage sources, $\mathbf{R}\mathbf{I} = \mathbf{V}_s$ where:

- $R_{kk}$ = sum of resistances in mesh $k$
- $R_{kj}$ = negative of resistance shared between meshes $k$ and $j$
- $V_{s,k}$ = sum of voltage sources driving mesh $k$ in the assumed direction

Mesh is generally easier when **there are few meshes** relative to nodes, or when most sources are **voltage sources**.

examples.q: A two-mesh circuit: Mesh 1 has 20 V source, 4 Ω, and the shared 6 Ω. Mesh 2 has the shared 6 Ω and 8 Ω. Both clockwise. Write the mesh equations.

pitfalls: Inconsistent mesh-current direction. Pick clockwise for all meshes and stick with it.
Forgetting that shared-resistor terms get the negative sign in by-inspection matrix form.

topics.title: Mesh Analysis with Current Sources (Supermesh)
topics.body:
When a **current source** is shared between two adjacent meshes, you can't write a standard KVL through it — the voltage across the source isn't known up front.

**The supermesh technique**: treat the two meshes plus the current source between them as one big 'supermesh', drawn around the outside *excluding* the shared current source. Write KVL around this supermesh boundary. Then add a constraint equation from the current source:

$$i_i - i_j = I_s$$

(sign per the source's arrow direction).

**Procedure**:

1. Identify any current source shared between two meshes.
2. For each such source, form a supermesh around the two meshes, excluding the source.
3. Write KVL for the supermesh.
4. Add the constraint equation $i_i - i_j = I_s$.
5. Write KVL normally for all non-supermesh meshes.

If the current source is between a mesh and the **outside** (so only one mesh touches it), that mesh's current is **directly known** ($i_k = I_s$) — no supermesh needed.
pitfalls: Including the current source's voltage in the supermesh KVL. The whole point of the supermesh is to step *around* the source.
Forgetting the constraint equation $i_i - i_j = I_s$. Without it, supermesh underdetermines the system by one equation.

topics.title: Nodal vs Mesh Analysis Comparison
topics.body:
Both methods solve the same circuit and give the same answer. Which is faster depends on the network's geometry and source mix.

**Prefer nodal when**:

- The circuit has fewer nodes than meshes.
- Most sources are *current sources*.
- You need a *voltage* answer directly (saves the conversion).
- The circuit is non-planar (mesh analysis only works on planar circuits anyway).

**Prefer mesh when**:

- The circuit has fewer meshes than nodes.
- Most sources are *voltage sources*.
- You need a *current* answer directly.

**Equation count comparison** for a circuit with $b$ branches, $n$ nodes, $\ell = b - n + 1$ meshes:

- Nodal: $n - 1$ equations
- Mesh: $\ell = b - n + 1$ equations

So if $n - 1 < b - n + 1$, i.e. $b > 2n - 2$, mesh is bigger and nodal wins.

**Practical advice**: count both quickly before starting. Don't half-finish mesh because you forgot to check that nodal would have been three equations smaller.

topics.title: Circuit Analysis by Inspection
topics.body:
For circuits restricted to **resistors + independent sources**, both nodal and mesh equations can be written down by inspection without going through the full KCL/KVL setup. This is much faster on exams.

**Nodal by inspection** — for $n - 1$ non-reference nodes:

$$\mathbf{G}\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{I}_s$$

- $G_{kk}$ = sum of all conductances ($1/R$) connected to node $k$.
- $G_{kj}$ = negative of conductance directly connecting nodes $k$ and $j$ (0 if not connected).
- $I_{s,k}$ = sum of independent current sources flowing **into** node $k$.

**Mesh by inspection** — for $\ell$ meshes (all currents assigned clockwise):

$$\mathbf{R}\mathbf{I} = \mathbf{V}_s$$

- $R_{kk}$ = sum of all resistances in mesh $k$.
- $R_{kj}$ = negative of resistance shared between meshes $k$ and $j$.
- $V_{s,k}$ = algebraic sum of voltage sources around mesh $k$ in the assumed direction.

Both matrices are **symmetric** ($G_{kj} = G_{jk}$, $R_{kj} = R_{jk}$) — a useful sanity check.

**Limitation**: by-inspection rules **don't apply** to circuits with dependent sources or ideal voltage/current sources that violate the by-inspection assumptions (use supernodes / supermeshes for those).

topics.title: Applications: DC Transistor Circuits
topics.body:
Bipolar junction transistors (BJTs) in DC bias analysis are a natural application of nodal and mesh techniques. The BJT itself is nonlinear, but in DC analysis we use a **piecewise linear model**:

- Base-emitter: a fixed voltage drop $V_{BE} \approx 0.7$ V (silicon) when on.
- Collector current: $I_C = \beta I_B$ where $\beta$ (or $h_{FE}$) is the current gain (typically 50–300).
- Emitter current: $I_E = I_B + I_C = (\beta + 1) I_B$.

Once you replace the transistor with these constraints, the surrounding network is purely linear and ordinary KVL/KCL analysis gives you the bias point ($V_C, V_B, V_E, I_C, I_B$).

**Why this matters**: every amplifier, every logic gate, every analog stage starts from a bias-point calculation. Mastering KCL/KVL with one or two transistors in the loop is the first real engineering application of the methods of analysis.

topics.title: Linearity Property and Superposition
topics.body:
A circuit is **linear** if it contains only linear elements (resistors, ideal sources, linear dependent sources, ideal capacitors and inductors). Linear means two things:

- **Homogeneity**: if you scale every independent source by a factor $k$, every voltage and current in the circuit scales by the same $k$.
- **Additivity**: the response to several sources acting together equals the sum of the responses to each source acting alone.

The **superposition theorem** is the additivity property made into a calculation method. For a linear circuit with multiple independent sources, **the voltage across (or current through) any element is the algebraic sum of contributions from each independent source considered separately, with all other independent sources deactivated**.

**Deactivating a source**:

- Independent **voltage** source → replace with a **short circuit** (0 V).
- Independent **current** source → replace with an **open circuit** (0 A).
- **Dependent** sources are *never* deactivated — they stay as-is throughout.

**When to use it**: when several independent sources of different types or frequencies drive a linear network, especially when one source is much easier to analyse alone.

examples.q: A load voltage is 4 V when only source $V_1$ acts, and 3 V when only $V_2$ acts (both polarities the same). What is the load voltage when both sources act together?

pitfalls: Deactivating dependent sources. Never do this — only independent sources are turned off.
Using superposition for *power* directly. Power is nonlinear in current and voltage; you must compute the full current/voltage first, then square it. $P \neq P_1 + P_2$ in general.

topics.title: Source Transformation
topics.body:
Any practical voltage source (an ideal source $V_s$ in **series** with $R_s$) is equivalent — at its external terminals — to a practical current source (ideal source $I_s$ in **parallel** with the same $R_s$). The transformation is:

$$I_s = \dfrac{V_s}{R_s}, \qquad R_s \text{ unchanged}$$

and the reverse:

$$V_s = I_s \cdot R_s$$

Polarity matters: the current source's arrow points **toward the + terminal** of the voltage source it replaces.

**Why it's useful**: by repeatedly transforming sources, you can often collapse a complex network of resistors and sources into a single source plus a single resistance — the same endpoint as Thévenin / Norton, but reached step by step.

**Limitations**:

- Doesn't apply to an **ideal** source (no internal resistance). You need a finite $R_s$.
- The transformed sources are equivalent **only at the external terminals** — internal currents and powers are different. So the power dissipated in $R_s$ is different in the two forms, even though everything outside is identical.

examples.q: Convert a 12 V source in series with 4 Ω to its current-source equivalent.
steps: $R_s$ stays the same and moves into parallel.
examples.answer: 3 A current source in parallel with 4 Ω

pitfalls: Forgetting that polarity matters. The current source arrow points toward what was the + terminal of the voltage source.
Treating internal power as the same in both forms. The external behaviour is identical, but the resistor's internal power is not.

topics.title: Thévenin's Theorem
topics.body:
**Thévenin's theorem** states that any two-terminal linear network — no matter how many sources and resistors — can be replaced **at those two terminals** by:

- A single voltage source $V_{Th}$ (the **Thévenin voltage**)
- in series with a single resistance $R_{Th}$ (the **Thévenin resistance**).

**Finding $V_{Th}$**: remove the load and measure (or compute) the **open-circuit voltage** at the terminals: $V_{Th} = V_{oc}$.

**Finding $R_{Th}$** (three methods, pick whichever fits):

1. **No dependent sources** — deactivate all independent sources (voltage → short, current → open) and compute the equivalent resistance at the terminals using series/parallel reduction.
2. **Has dependent sources** — apply a test source $V_T$ at the terminals (with all independent sources still deactivated), compute the resulting test current $I_T$, then $R_{Th} = V_T / I_T$.
3. **Open-short method** — $R_{Th} = V_{oc} / I_{sc}$ where $I_{sc}$ is the short-circuit current at the terminals. Works whether or not dependent sources are present.

**Why it's useful**: once you have $(V_{Th}, R_{Th})$, you can hook up any load $R_L$ and instantly find load current and voltage:

$$I_L = \dfrac{V_{Th}}{R_{Th} + R_L}, \qquad V_L = \dfrac{R_L}{R_{Th} + R_L} \cdot V_{Th}$$

No need to re-solve the whole network for every new load value.

examples.q: A network has $V_{oc} = 18$ V at its terminals and $I_{sc} = 3$ A. Find $R_{Th}$.

pitfalls: Deactivating dependent sources when finding $R_{Th}$. Use the test-source method instead.
Forgetting that Thévenin is equivalent **only at the chosen terminals**. Internal node voltages and branch currents inside the original network are not preserved.

topics.title: Norton's Theorem
topics.body:
**Norton's theorem** is the dual of Thévenin. Any two-terminal linear network is equivalent to:

- A single current source $I_N$ (the **Norton current**)
- in parallel with a single resistance $R_N$.

**Finding $I_N$**: short the terminals and measure the **short-circuit current**: $I_N = I_{sc}$.

**Finding $R_N$**: same as $R_{Th}$ — by Thévenin / Norton equivalence, $R_N = R_{Th}$ always.

**Conversion between Thévenin and Norton** (it's just a source transformation):

$$V_{Th} = I_N \cdot R_N, \qquad I_N = \dfrac{V_{Th}}{R_{Th}}, \qquad R_{Th} = R_N$$

Use **Thévenin** when the rest of the circuit attached to the terminals is dominated by voltage-source thinking (series loops). Use **Norton** when current-source thinking (parallel branches) is more natural. They contain identical information; pick whichever simplifies the next step.

examples.q: A network has $V_{Th} = 36$ V and $R_{Th} = 12$ Ω. Find its Norton equivalent.

pitfalls: Stating $R_N \neq R_{Th}$. They're always equal — the same network's equivalent resistance.
Using $V_{Th}$ in a Norton diagram (or vice versa). Match the source type to the diagram type.

topics.title: Maximum Power Transfer
topics.body:
Given a fixed Thévenin source $(V_{Th}, R_{Th})$ driving a variable load $R_L$, how do you choose $R_L$ to extract the maximum power?

Power delivered to $R_L$:

$$P_L = i^{2} R_L = \left(\dfrac{V_{Th}}{R_{Th} + R_L}\right)^{2} R_L$$

Differentiate with respect to $R_L$, set $dP_L/dR_L = 0$, and you get the **Maximum Power Transfer Theorem**:

$$\boxed{R_L = R_{Th}}$$

At this load:

$$P_\text{max} = \dfrac{V_{Th}^{\,2}}{4 R_{Th}}$$

**Efficiency at maximum power transfer is only 50%** — half the source power goes into $R_L$, the other half is dissipated in $R_{Th}$. This is fine for signal-transfer applications (audio, RF), where what matters is the signal *amplitude* delivered. It's **not** what you want for power-delivery applications (electric grid), where efficiency matters more than raw power — there you want $R_L \gg R_{Th}$, giving low loss in the source but also low absolute power.

**Procedure to apply it**:

1. Find $V_{Th}$ and $R_{Th}$ at the load's terminals.
2. Set $R_L = R_{Th}$.
3. $P_\text{max} = V_{Th}^2 / (4 R_{Th})$.

examples.q: A Thévenin source has $V_{Th} = 20$ V and $R_{Th} = 10$ Ω. What load gives maximum power, and what is that power?

pitfalls: Confusing maximum-power transfer with maximum efficiency. They're different goals.
Forgetting that $R_{Th}$ here is the equivalent resistance of *everything except the load*. Compute it correctly first.

topics.title: Applications: Source Modelling, Resistance Measurement
topics.body:
**Source modelling**. Real batteries, generators, and amplifier outputs are not ideal sources. A 9 V battery doesn't deliver 9 V at every load — drop a serious current and the terminal voltage sags. Modelling a real source as a Thévenin (or Norton) equivalent lets you predict that sag:

$$V_\text{terminal} = V_{Th} - I \cdot R_{Th}$$

A typical AA battery: $V_{Th} \approx 1.5$ V, $R_{Th} \approx 0.15$ Ω. At 10 A short-circuit current... actually it can't deliver 10 A; the terminal voltage would collapse first.

**Resistance measurement by Wheatstone bridge**. Four resistors in a diamond — when the bridge is balanced, the galvanometer (between the two midpoints) reads zero current, and $R_1/R_2 = R_3/R_4$. Unknown resistance can be solved if the other three are known. The circuit is a classic textbook example of Thévenin analysis: to find the galvanometer current when the bridge is *not* balanced, find the Thévenin equivalent at the two midpoints and connect the galvanometer as a load.

**Multimeter ohmmeter mode**: passes a small known current through the unknown resistor, measures the voltage across it, computes $R = V/I$. Internally a current-source + voltmeter implementation of Ohm's law.

key_formulas.formula_ascii: v = v1 + v2 + ... (one source at a time)

key_formulas.formula_ascii: P_max when R_L = R_Th; P_max = V_Th²/(4R_Th)

topics.title: Capacitor: Structure & v-i Relationship
topics.body:
A **capacitor** is two conducting plates separated by a non-conducting dielectric. When voltage is applied, positive charge accumulates on one plate and equal negative charge on the other, storing energy in the electric field between them.

**Capacitance** is the ratio of stored charge to applied voltage:

$$C = \dfrac{Q}{V}$$

Unit: farad (F), where $1 \text{ F} = 1 \text{ C/V}$. One farad is huge — practical values are in µF (microfarad, $10^{-6}$), nF ($10^{-9}$), and pF ($10^{-12}$).

**Parallel-plate formula**:

$$C = \varepsilon \dfrac{A}{d} = \varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r \dfrac{A}{d}$$

where $A$ is the plate area, $d$ is the plate separation, $\varepsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{-12}$ F/m is the permittivity of free space, and $\varepsilon_r$ is the relative permittivity of the dielectric (1 for air; ~2.5 for polyester film; ~7 for mica; ~10 000 for some ceramics).

**The fundamental v-i relationship**:

$$i = C \dfrac{dv}{dt}$$

Current flows only while voltage is *changing*. Three immediate consequences:

1. **DC steady state**: $dv/dt = 0$, so $i = 0$. A capacitor behaves as an **open circuit** to DC.
2. **Voltage cannot change instantaneously**: a step change in $v$ would require infinite current. So $v_C(0^+) = v_C(0^-)$ across any switching event.
3. **AC reactance**: in a sinusoidal AC circuit, the higher the frequency, the more current flows for the same voltage — capacitors *pass* high frequencies and *block* DC.

**Integrating** the v-i relationship gives the voltage in terms of past current:

$$v(t) = \dfrac{1}{C} \int_{-\infty}^{t} i(\tau) \, d\tau = v(0) + \dfrac{1}{C} \int_{0}^{t} i(\tau) \, d\tau$$

The capacitor 'remembers' all the charge that's ever flowed into it (until it leaks away).

examples.q: The voltage across a 50 µF capacitor varies as $v(t) = 20\cos(1000 t)$ V. Find $i(t)$.

pitfalls: Trying to apply Ohm's law $v = iR$ to a capacitor. Capacitors don't have resistance in this sense — their v-i is *differential*.
Forgetting capacitor voltage is continuous across a switching instant. The current can jump; the voltage cannot.

topics.title: Energy Stored in a Capacitor
topics.body:
The instantaneous power delivered to a capacitor is $p = v \cdot i = v \cdot C \, dv/dt$. Integrating from zero voltage to some final $V$ gives the energy stored in the electric field:

$$W = \dfrac{1}{2} C V^{2}$$

Equivalent forms:

$$W = \dfrac{Q^{2}}{2C} = \dfrac{1}{2} Q V$$

Energy is in joules. Notable facts:

- A capacitor **stores** energy when charging (energy goes from source into the field) and **returns** it when discharging — unlike a resistor, which dissipates it as heat.
- Energy scales as $V^{2}$. Doubling the voltage *quadruples* the stored energy. This is why high-voltage capacitor banks (defibrillators, photoflash, industrial pulsed power) can be dangerous even at moderate capacitance.
- A 1 F supercapacitor charged to 5 V stores 12.5 J — comparable to a small battery, deliverable in milliseconds.

**Always treat any large or unknown capacitor as charged** until you've shorted it through a resistor. Even 'discharged' capacitors can self-recharge from dielectric absorption.

examples.q: Energy stored in a 470 µF capacitor charged to 25 V.

pitfalls: Using $W = \frac{1}{2}CV$ (missing the square). The energy is quadratic in voltage.
Forgetting that large capacitors can deliver dangerous current bursts even if their voltage doesn't look high.

topics.title: Series and Parallel Capacitors
topics.body:
**Parallel capacitors**. When connected in parallel, capacitors share the same voltage but store separate charges. Equivalent capacitance:

$$C_\text{eq} = C_1 + C_2 + \cdots + C_n$$

Plate areas effectively add — bigger total area for the same plate separation gives a bigger capacitor.

**Series capacitors**. When in series, the same charge $Q$ accumulates on each (charge has nowhere else to go), but the voltage splits inversely with capacitance. Equivalent:

$$\dfrac{1}{C_\text{eq}} = \dfrac{1}{C_1} + \dfrac{1}{C_2} + \cdots + \dfrac{1}{C_n}$$

For exactly two:

$$C_\text{eq} = \dfrac{C_1 C_2}{C_1 + C_2}$$

Series equivalent is *smaller* than any individual capacitor — opposite to resistors.

**Energy split in series**: same $Q$ on all → smaller $C$ stores *more* energy ($W = Q^2/2C$).

**Energy split in parallel**: same $V$ across all → larger $C$ stores *more* energy ($W = \frac{1}{2}CV^2$).

**Why use series of capacitors?** Two 200 V capacitors in series can handle 400 V across the pair (with a balancing resistor network in practice). This is how high-voltage capacitor banks are assembled from lower-rated units.

examples.q: $C_1 = 6$ µF and $C_2 = 3$ µF in series. Find $C_\text{eq}$.

pitfalls: Adding series capacitors directly. Series of capacitors uses the *reciprocal* formula, like parallel resistors.
Forgetting that the smaller capacitor in a series pair takes the larger voltage. Critical for voltage-rating choices.

topics.title: Capacitor Classification, Labelling, and Standard Values
topics.body:
**Major types by dielectric**:

| Type | Dielectric | Range | Voltage | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ceramic (MLCC, disc) | Class 1 NP0 / Class 2 X7R | 1 pF – 100 µF | 6.3 V – 1 kV | Decoupling, RF, timing |
| Aluminum electrolytic | $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ (polarised) | 0.1 µF – 1 F | 6.3 – 450 V | Bulk smoothing |
| Tantalum | $\text{Ta}_2\text{O}_5$ (polarised) | 0.1 – 1000 µF | 2 – 50 V | Compact filtering |
| Film (polyester / polypropylene / PTFE) | Plastic film | 1 nF – 100 µF | 50 V – 2 kV | Audio, snubbers, precision |
| Mica | Natural/silvered mica | 1 pF – 10 nF | 100 V – kV | HF, high-precision |
| Supercapacitor | Electric double layer | 0.1 – 3000 F | 2.5 – 5 V | Energy buffering |

**Polarised** types (electrolytic, tantalum) must be connected with correct polarity — reverse voltage destroys the dielectric and the capacitor can rupture.

**Labelling** — three-digit codes used on small ceramics and films give the value in **picofarads**: first two digits are significant figures, third is the power of ten multiplier.

| Code | Value |
|---|---|
| 104 | $10 \times 10^4$ pF = 100,000 pF = 100 nF = 0.1 µF |
| 473 | $47 \times 10^3$ pF = 47 nF |
| 220 | $22 \times 10^0$ pF = 22 pF |
| 2A104K | 100 V, 0.1 µF, ±10% |

**Tolerance letter** (often follows the code): J = ±5%, K = ±10%, M = ±20%, F = ±1%, D = ±0.5 pF.

**Standard E-series values** — capacitors come in geometrically-spaced 'preferred values' so the tolerance bands tile the range. **E12** base values per decade: 10, 12, 15, 18, 22, 27, 33, 39, 47, 56, 68, 82. Common stock values you'll actually see in a parts drawer: 0.1, 0.22, 0.47, 1, 2.2, 4.7, 10, 22, 47, 100, 220, 470 µF, and similar across nF and pF.
pitfalls: Connecting a polarised capacitor backwards. The negative leg is marked with a stripe (electrolytic) or a bar (tantalum). Reverse voltage = damage.
Treating the printed value as exact. A '100 µF' ±20% electrolytic may actually be anywhere from 80 to 120 µF.

topics.title: Charging Phase of a Capacitor (RC Circuit)
topics.body:
Connect an uncharged capacitor $C$ through a resistor $R$ to a DC source $V_s$ by closing a switch at $t = 0$. The capacitor starts at 0 V (it can't change voltage instantly), so the entire $V_s$ momentarily appears across $R$, giving an initial current $V_s/R$. As charge accumulates on the capacitor, its voltage rises, the voltage across $R$ falls, and current decreases — until eventually $v_C = V_s$ and current stops.

**Governing differential equation** (from KVL):

$$RC \dfrac{dv}{dt} + v = V_s$$

**Solution** for the charging response:

$$v_C(t) = V_s \left(1 - e^{-t/RC}\right)$$

$$i(t) = \dfrac{V_s}{R} \, e^{-t/RC}$$

The **time constant** $\tau = RC$ is the natural timescale of the circuit. R in ohms, C in farads, $\tau$ in seconds.

**Behavioural milestones**:

| Time | $v_C$ | $i$ |
|---|---|---|
| $0^+$ | 0 | $V_s/R$ (peak) |
| 1τ | 63.2% of $V_s$ | 36.8% of peak |
| 2τ | 86.5% | 13.5% |
| 3τ | 95.0% | 5.0% |
| 5τ | 99.3% (≈ 'fully charged') | 0.7% |

Practical rule: capacitor is considered **fully charged after 5τ**.

examples.q: A 100 µF capacitor charges through a 10 kΩ resistor from a 12 V source. Find τ and the voltage at $t = 1$ s.

pitfalls: Treating the initial current as something other than $V_s/R$. At $t = 0^+$, the capacitor is a short circuit (zero voltage), so the full source drives R alone.
Forgetting that 5τ is a rule of thumb. In high-precision settings (oscillator timing) you may need 10τ or more.

topics.title: Discharging Phase of a Capacitor
topics.body:
Take a capacitor previously charged to $V_0$ and remove the source — close a switch that connects only $R$ and $C$ in a loop. The stored charge on the capacitor now drives current *backward* through the resistor, gradually returning the capacitor to zero.

**Governing differential equation**:

$$RC \dfrac{dv}{dt} + v = 0$$

**Solution**:

$$v_C(t) = V_0 \, e^{-t/RC}$$

$$i(t) = -\dfrac{V_0}{R} \, e^{-t/RC}$$

The negative sign on $i$ shows the **current reverses direction** relative to charging — it now flows *out* of the capacitor's positive plate.

**Milestones**:

| Time | $v_C$ (% of $V_0$) |
|---|---|
| 1τ | 36.8% |
| 2τ | 13.5% |
| 3τ | 5.0% |
| 4τ | 1.8% |
| 5τ | 0.7% (≈ 'fully discharged') |

**Energy bookkeeping during discharge**: every joule of stored capacitor energy ends up dissipated as heat in the resistor. The total heat = $\frac{1}{2}CV_0^2$, regardless of $R$. (Smaller $R$ = faster discharge but same total heat.)

examples.q: A 100 µF capacitor charged to 12 V discharges through 10 kΩ. Find the current at $t = 0^+$ and the voltage at $t = 2$ s.

pitfalls: Reversing the sign of the discharge current. By convention, current during discharge is *opposite* to the charging direction.
Computing total energy dissipated using $i^2 R \cdot t$. The current decays exponentially — you'd have to integrate. Use $\frac{1}{2}CV_0^2$ for the total directly.

chapters.title: First-Order Circuits

topics.title: Source-Free RC Circuit (Natural Response)
topics.body:
A **source-free** circuit has no independent source acting on it — only stored energy in a capacitor (or inductor) and a path for it to dissipate. The resulting response is called the **natural response**: how the circuit relaxes back to zero on its own.

For a source-free RC circuit with the capacitor initially charged to $V_0$:

$$v_C(t) = V_0 \, e^{-t/\tau}, \qquad \tau = RC$$

$$i(t) = -\dfrac{V_0}{R} \, e^{-t/\tau}$$

**Why exponential?** The defining equation $RC \, dv/dt + v = 0$ has the form 'rate of change of $v$ is proportional to $v$'. The only function whose derivative is proportional to itself is the exponential.

**Properties of the natural response**:

- Falls to zero asymptotically — never quite reaches it.
- Independent of how the capacitor was charged. All that matters for $t > 0$ is the initial value $V_0$.
- The shape (exponential) is identical for every source-free first-order circuit. Only the time constant $\tau$ changes.

This is the 'dying away' part of any switching transient.

examples.q: A 200 µF capacitor charged to 24 V is allowed to discharge through 50 kΩ at $t = 0$. When does $v_C$ fall to 5 V?

pitfalls: Forgetting that the natural response has no source term. It's purely the relaxation of stored energy.
Mixing units. R in kΩ and C in µF gives $\tau$ in ms (the $10^3$ and $10^{-6}$ multiply to $10^{-3}$).

topics.title: Singularity Functions (Step, Impulse, Ramp)
topics.body:
Switching events in real circuits are idealised as **singularity functions** — mathematical shapes that capture sudden changes cleanly.

**Unit step function** $u(t)$:

$$u(t) = \begin{cases} 0, & t < 0 \\ 1, & t > 0 \end{cases}$$

Models 'turning on' a source at $t = 0$. A source $V_s \cdot u(t)$ delivers 0 V before $t = 0$ and $V_s$ afterwards. Shifted version $u(t - t_0)$ turns on at $t = t_0$.

**Unit impulse (delta) function** $\delta(t)$:

$$\delta(t) = \dfrac{du(t)}{dt}, \qquad \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(t) \, dt = 1$$

An infinitely tall, infinitesimally narrow spike of unit area. Models an instantaneous charge injection or a hammer-blow.

**Unit ramp function** $r(t)$:

$$r(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{t} u(\tau) \, d\tau = t \, u(t)$$

Linearly rising signal starting at $t = 0$. Models a linearly increasing voltage or current.

**Relationships**:

$$\dfrac{dr}{dt} = u, \qquad \dfrac{du}{dt} = \delta$$

Each one is the derivative of the next. They're the building blocks of more complex transient inputs.

topics.title: Step Response of an RC Circuit
topics.body:
The **step response** is what happens when you apply a step input to a circuit that was previously at some initial state. For an RC circuit driven by a step source $V_s \cdot u(t)$, the capacitor's voltage transitions from its initial value $V_0$ to its final steady-state value $V_s$:

$$\boxed{v_C(t) = V_f + (V_0 - V_f) \, e^{-t/\tau}}$$

for $t \ge 0$, where $V_f = V_s$ is the final value and $V_0$ is the initial value.

**Three special cases**:

- $V_0 = 0, V_f = V_s$ → pure charging from zero: $v_C(t) = V_s(1 - e^{-t/\tau})$.
- $V_0 = V_s, V_f = 0$ → pure discharging: $v_C(t) = V_s \, e^{-t/\tau}$.
- $V_0 \ne 0, V_f \ne 0$ → general transition between two non-zero levels.

**Decomposition into natural + forced response**:

The step response is the sum of the **natural response** (the circuit's tendency to decay) and the **forced response** (steady-state value driven by the source):

$$v_C(t) = \underbrace{V_f}_{\text{forced}} + \underbrace{(V_0 - V_f) e^{-t/\tau}}_{\text{natural}}$$

**Three steps to solve any step-response problem**:

1. Find the **initial value** $V_0 = v_C(0^-) = v_C(0^+)$ — capacitor voltage just before (and so just after) switching.
2. Find the **final value** $V_f$ — capacitor voltage as $t \to \infty$ in the new configuration (capacitor acts as open circuit at DC steady state).
3. Find the **time constant** $\tau = RC$, using the Thévenin resistance seen from the capacitor's terminals.

examples.q: A 1 µF capacitor is initially charged to 4 V. At $t = 0$ it is connected through 50 kΩ to a 10 V source. Find $v_C(t)$.
steps: Final value: $V_f = 10$ V (no current flows in steady state, all source voltage on C).

pitfalls: Mixing up initial and final values. $V_0$ is just before switching (preserved by capacitor continuity); $V_f$ is the new steady state after switching.
Computing τ using the wrong resistance. After switching, find the Thévenin equivalent at the capacitor's terminals — that's the R for τ.

topics.title: Applications: Delay Circuits, Photoflash, Relays
topics.body:
First-order RC behaviour shows up everywhere a known *delay* or *energy buildup* is needed.

**Delay circuits**. A simple RC timer fires when the capacitor reaches a threshold voltage. The delay time is determined by $\tau = RC$. For example, a 555-timer in monostable mode produces a pulse of duration $T \approx 1.1 \, RC$ — one pin samples the rising capacitor voltage, fires when it hits 2/3 of supply, and resets.

**Camera photoflash**. A photoflash unit stores energy in a large capacitor (e.g. 250 µF at 300 V → $W = \frac{1}{2}CV^2 = 11.25$ J) and dumps that energy through a xenon flash tube in roughly 1 ms. Peak power is enormous (~10 kW) even though the average power from the small battery is modest. The capacitor stores slowly (over seconds) and releases fast — energy-density transformation by time scaling.

**Relay drive circuits**. A capacitor in parallel with a relay coil provides a brief current boost to ensure clean closure, then the steady-state current from the source keeps the relay held. The capacitor also reduces contact bounce-induced switching noise.

**Automobile ignition**. The classical Kettering ignition system uses a capacitor (condenser) to absorb the back-EMF from the ignition coil when the breaker points open, preventing the points from arcing. The capacitor sees a sharp $dV/dt$ event each time the coil's stored magnetic energy collapses — a classic transient.

**Why first-order analysis matters**: every one of these is solved with $v(t) = V_f + (V_0 - V_f) e^{-t/\tau}$. Master that single formula and a huge family of practical circuits opens up.
